intro: Read the deck for the rules and these notes for the thinking. The notes explain each slide, give you something to remember and warn you where people slip. The subject touches real harm, so pause whenever you need to. Try each section exercise before you read its answer, then test yourself with the recall questions.

sections.title: Orientation
sections.big_idea: Safeguarding rests on one idea, **the abuse of unequal power**, and on one rule of mindset: assume it can happen here.
in_plain_words: Safeguarding is how organisations make sure their staff, operations and programmes do no harm to the people they work with. Under that umbrella sit child protection, protection of at-risk adults and protection from sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment, grouped as SEAH. It protects two overlapping groups: the people we serve, and the people we work with.

Underneath every rule is power. When one person controls another's food, shelter, medicine, job or grade, apparent consent cannot be freely given, so the first question is whether there was a power imbalance. Words carry safety too: say survivor, say alleged, believe without judging and never blame. Five ground rules guide the course, starting with **it can happen here**, and every staff member shares the duty.

key_terms.meaning: An organisation's duty to make sure its work does no harm to the people it works with.
Protection from sexual exploitation and abuse of the people we serve.
Sexual exploitation, abuse and harassment: the umbrella acronym.
A person who has experienced sexual violence or exploitation; the preferred word.
When someone tells you they have experienced or witnessed harm.
The trained person who receives and channels safeguarding concerns.

worked_example.title: Which letters apply?
worked_example.setup: Use the question on slide 21 (who is being harmed, and by whom?) on four invented cases.
steps: A field officer asks a beneficiary for a favour to keep her on a list: an affected person harmed by staff, so PSEA.
A manager makes sexual comments to a junior colleague: staff harmed by staff, so sexual harassment.
A volunteer sends private messages to a child in a project: an affected person harmed by associated personnel, so PSEA, with child safeguarding on top.
A colleague repeatedly propositions another colleague: staff harmed by staff, so sexual harassment.
All four are SEAH, the combined acronym.
worked_example.answer: Cases 1 and 3 are PSEA, cases 2 and 4 are sexual harassment, and all four are SEAH.

mistakes: Treating safeguarding as the focal point's job. It belongs to every staff member.
Opening with 'was there consent?' The right first question is whether there was a power imbalance.
Using 'victim' or naming a perpetrator loosely. Say survivor, and say alleged until a finding is made.
Believing 'not in our organisation'. That belief is the condition under which harm continues.

recall.q: Define safeguarding in a sentence.
recall.a: The responsibility of organisations to make sure their staff, operations and programmes do no harm to the people they work with.

recall.q: How do PSEA and sexual harassment differ?
recall.a: PSEA is harm by personnel to the people served. Sexual harassment is harm between staff.

recall.q: Why is 'was there consent?' the wrong first question?
recall.a: Where one person controls another's access to what they need, consent cannot be freely given.

recall.q: Which ground rule calls silence that shields an abuser complicity?
recall.a: Confidentiality protects survivors.

sections.title: Definitions
sections.big_idea: SEAH is three harms under one umbrella. **Ask who is being harmed, and by whom**, because that decides which policy and response apply.
in_plain_words: Sexual exploitation is any actual or attempted abuse of a position of vulnerability, differential power or trust for sexual purposes. Sexual abuse is actual or threatened physical intrusion of a sexual nature, by force or under unequal or coercive conditions. Sexual harassment is unwelcome sexual conduct that creates an intimidating, hostile or offensive environment, usually between staff. All three rest on abuse of power.

PSEA protects affected populations from aid workers. Sexual harassment falls under workplace policy, in India the PoSH Act 2013. Misfiling one into the other's process can leave a survivor unprotected. A child is anyone under 18, with no consent possible and no defence for mistaken age, and India's POCSO Act 2012 adds mandatory reporting. These are **working definitions, and criminal law governs** where a crime may have occurred.

diagram.note: SEA targets affected people (PSEA); SH targets colleagues (workplace policy)

key_terms.meaning: Abuse of vulnerability, power or trust for sexual purposes (UN definition).
Actual or threatened physical intrusion of a sexual nature.
Unwelcome sexual conduct creating an intimidating or hostile environment.
Linking a promotion, contract or grade to sexual compliance.
Anyone under 18, whatever the local age of majority or consent.
An adult at heightened risk who is less able to protect themselves.

worked_example.title: Route two complaints
worked_example.setup: Two invented complaints arrive on one day. Use the table on slide 20 to route each.
steps: Complaint 1: a beneficiary says a staff member demanded sex to release her rations. Harmed: an affected person. Caused by: an aid worker.
Route 1 to the PSEA policy, code of conduct and referral pathways, under ST/SGB/2003/13, the IASC principles and the CHS.
Complaint 2: a junior colleague says her manager linked her contract renewal to sexual compliance. Harmed: staff. Caused by: a manager.
Route 2 to the anti-harassment or PoSH policy and internal committee, under labour law and, in India, the PoSH Act 2013.
Misfiling either one into the other's process can leave a survivor unprotected.
worked_example.answer: Complaint 1 is PSEA and complaint 2 is sexual harassment. Both are SEAH and both are unacceptable.

mistakes: Filing a beneficiary's complaint into an HR process, or the reverse.
Treating payment as making an exchange acceptable. The definition prohibits exactly that exchange.
Offering 'I thought she was older' as a defence. Mistaken age is no defence.
Using the organisational definition as if it were a court's finding.

recall.q: Which UN document defines sexual exploitation and abuse?
recall.a: The Secretary-General's Bulletin, ST/SGB/2003/13, Section 1.

recall.q: Who counts as a child under these rules?
recall.a: Any person under 18, regardless of local age of majority or consent.

recall.q: Which law governs workplace sexual harassment in India?
recall.a: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013 (the PoSH Act), which requires an Internal Committee.

recall.q: Name the three kinds of power gap on slide 19.
recall.a: Positional, relational and situational.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.big_idea: Rules exist because **need plus power is the raw material of exploitation**, and silence protects the abuser. Few reports signal unsafe channels.
in_plain_words: In 2010-11, after the Haiti earthquake, senior Oxfam staff used sex workers. An internal inquiry was not made public, and The Times exposed the story in February 2018. The scandal lay in the handling as well as the abuse. The sector responded with parliamentary scrutiny, the October 2018 London Safeguarding Summit, the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme and donor conditions. Do no harm is the foundation.

Providers hold food, cash, shelter and jobs, while recipients fear complaining will cut off aid. That is why exploitation is badly under-reported: fear of losing aid, retaliation, stigma, no safe channel, disbelief and normalisation. Few reports are no evidence of low prevalence. In South Asia, inequality, recurrent crises, a large informal workforce and stigma raise the risk. **Zero tolerance means zero tolerance of inaction**, and it promises no absence of incidents.

key_terms.meaning: The first responsibility of anyone offering help: help must not become harm.
Zero tolerance of inaction: every concern is taken seriously and acted on.
Few reports because channels are unsafe, unknown or distrusted.
A contract term passing the same standards to every partner and sub-grantee.
Concealing a case to protect reputation, which compounds the harm.

worked_example.title: Read a report count
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: three field offices report 0, 3 and 12 safeguarding concerns in a year, and leadership proposes praising the office with none.
steps: Total concerns: 0 + 3 + 12 = 15.
Slide 29: few reports are no evidence of low prevalence, so zero asks a question.
Check the barriers in the zero office: fear of losing aid, retaliation, stigma, no safe channel, disbelief, normalisation.
Slide 33: a rising number of reports through safe channels is often a sign the system is working, so 12 may mean the channels work.
Audit the zero office's channels before offering any praise.
worked_example.answer: Treat zero as a question about safe channels, and expect a mature system to show more reports.

mistakes: Reading 'no reports' as 'no problem'.
Reading zero tolerance as zero incidents, which pushes problems underground.
Protecting reputation at a survivor's expense. The damage from a cover-up is always worse.
Treating donor rules as paperwork. Safeguarding capacity is now a condition of funding.

recall.q: What went wrong in Haiti beyond the abuse itself?
recall.a: A flawed investigation, too little done to establish whether minors were involved, and a cover-up that compounded harm.

recall.q: Name three barriers to reporting.
recall.a: Any three of: fear of losing aid, fear of retaliation, stigma and shame, no safe channel, disbelief, normalisation.

recall.q: What does zero tolerance mean?
recall.a: Zero tolerance of inaction. It does not mean zero incidents.

recall.q: Name three things donors now require.
recall.a: Any three of: policy and procedures, named responsibility, safe recruitment, flow-down clauses, incident reporting within timelines.

sections.title: The standards and framework
sections.big_idea: Four layers nest: **Bulletin, IASC principles, CHS, then your own code**. None is law alone, and the code you signed is what binds you.
in_plain_words: The UN Secretary-General's Bulletin, ST/SGB/2003/13, supplies the source definitions and prohibitions. The IASC six core principles turn them into shared conduct rules: gross misconduct, no sex with children, no exchange for sex, no relationships that abuse power, a duty to report and a duty to sustain the environment. Principles 5 and 6 make safeguarding active.

The Core Humanitarian Standard has nine commitments on quality and accountability to affected people, including do no harm and safe complaints. A complaints mechanism must be known, accessible, safe and responsive, and it must welcome SEAH complaints explicitly. Reporting is mandatory, even across agencies, and you report suspicion without proof. Duty of care runs to the people served and to staff. These instruments bind through contracts, donor conditions and codes of conduct, so **your own code is the governing document**.

diagram.caption: each layer builds on the one before

key_terms.meaning: Six core principles on sexual exploitation and abuse, the sector baseline.
The UN Bulletin that sets the source definitions and prohibitions.
Core Humanitarian Standard: nine commitments on quality and accountability.
A duty to protect the people served and the staff who serve them.
The obligation to report known or suspected SEAH through your mechanism.
Conduct, such as SEA, that is grounds for termination.

worked_example.title: Match the case to the principle
worked_example.setup: Six invented situations. Use slides 36 and 37 to name the IASC principle each one engages.
steps: A worker says he believed a girl was over 18: principle 2, because mistaken belief about age is no defence.
An officer offers extra rations for sex: principle 3, exchange for sex, including assistance that is due.
A senior manager starts a relationship with a beneficiary using his rank: principle 4.
A driver sees a colleague's conduct and says nothing: principle 5, the duty to report, even about another agency's worker.
A country director ignores weak systems: principle 6, managers at all levels must support systems that keep the environment safe.
Any act of exploitation or abuse by a humanitarian worker: principle 1, gross misconduct.
worked_example.answer: Principles 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 1 in order. Principles 5 and 6 are the two that require you to act beyond your own conduct.

mistakes: Thinking the Bulletin, IASC principles or CHS are law in themselves. They bind through contracts and codes.
Reading 'strongly discouraged' in the Bulletin as permission. Many codes prohibit such relationships outright.
Waiting for proof before reporting. You report suspicions.
Running a complaints channel that does not explicitly welcome SEAH complaints. It will miss them.

recall.q: Which two IASC principles make safeguarding active?
recall.a: Principle 5, the duty to report, and principle 6, the duty to sustain the environment.

recall.q: What four features should a complaints mechanism have?
recall.a: Known, accessible, safe and confidential, and responsive.

recall.q: Does the duty to report apply to staff of another organisation?
recall.a: Yes. The duty applies even if the person concerned works for a different organisation.

recall.q: What document binds you day to day?
recall.a: Your own code of conduct and national law, which draw on the global standards.

sections.title: The red lines and code of conduct
sections.big_idea: The red lines are absolute and short. The hard part is the **everyday boundaries**: lifts, phone numbers, favours and home visits.
in_plain_words: A code of conduct turns the standards into personal rules. The red lines are: no sexual activity with anyone under 18, no exchange of aid, money, jobs or services for sex, no sexual relationships with beneficiaries, no sexual harassment, and a duty to report. Crossing them is serious misconduct whatever the context, consent claims or seniority. A relationship that arises must be declared.

Around the red lines sit softer rules. Declare conflicts of interest and step back from the decision. Refuse gifts and favours that create obligation, and never give them to select individuals. Keep devices, messaging and photography within the same red lines, with consent and dignity. Day to day, meet in open places, keep contact professional, treat everyone equally and use the test: **would I be comfortable if my manager, the community and the survivor's family saw this?**

key_terms.meaning: An absolute prohibition; crossing it is serious misconduct.
A personal tie that could improperly influence a decision in your role.
Gifts and favours that build obligation and lower defences before exploitation.
Explaining how an image will be used, in a language the person understands.
A signed personal commitment gathering the red lines in one document.

worked_example.title: Declare, don't decide
worked_example.setup: Invented: a field officer's cousin applies to a cash programme he helps select, and a beneficiary offers him food after enrolment.
steps: The relative is a conflict of interest: a personal tie could improperly influence selection.
Apply the rule from slide 49: declare, don't decide. Tell your manager and step back from the decision.
The food is a gift from someone who depends on his decisions. It creates a debt that can be called in later.
Decline it, and tell your manager if it keeps happening.
Run the test from slide 54: would he be comfortable if his manager, the community and the survivor's family saw what he is doing?
worked_example.answer: Declare the relationship, step back from selection and refuse the gift. Declaring protects him as much as the community.

mistakes: Answering 'but we're in love' as if feelings settle the power gap.
Believing a payment makes an exchange acceptable.
Sharing survivor details on personal devices or in informal chat groups.
Publishing a photo without informed consent, or after the person has asked for its removal.

recall.q: Name the five red lines.
recall.a: No sex with under-18s, no exchange for sex, no sexual relationships with beneficiaries, no sexual harassment, and a duty to report.

recall.q: What does 'declare, don't decide' mean?
recall.a: Disclose the connection to your manager and step back from the decision.

recall.q: If you are unsure whether someone is over 18 at work, what do you do?
recall.a: Treat them as a child. There is no acceptable margin of error.

recall.q: What is the test for everyday boundaries?
recall.a: Would I be comfortable if my manager, the community and the survivor's family saw exactly what I am doing?

sections.title: Recognising and receiving
sections.big_idea: Receiving a disclosure well means **safety first, listen, believe, explain your duty and refer**. Restraint is part of care.
in_plain_words: Exploitation shows up as patterns: favouritism, private meetings and secrecy in a colleague, and fear, withdrawal or unexplained goods in an affected person. Signs prove nothing alone. A disclosure may be direct, hinted, third-party or behavioural, and a person may test you with a small disclosure first. Your response to that first hint decides whether the full story is ever told.

The survivor-centred approach rests on four principles: safety, confidentiality, respect and non-discrimination. In practice, believe, restore control, give informed choice and do no further harm. Be honest about your reporting duty, never promise secrecy you cannot keep, and never investigate. With a child, best interests and mandatory reporting shape the response. In the first hours, secure safety, offer time-sensitive medical care, refer with consent, then report. **Look after yourself** too, because secondary trauma is real.

key_terms.meaning: Putting the survivor's rights, needs and wishes at the centre of every decision.
A hint such as 'a friend of mine...', testing whether it is safe to say more.
Emotional harm to responders from receiving disclosures of abuse.
The person alleged to have caused harm, until a finding is made.
The principle guiding every decision about a child survivor.

worked_example.title: Sort three replies
worked_example.setup: Use the table on slide 62 to judge three invented replies to a disclosure.
steps: 'Are you sure? That is not like him.' Avoid it: it voices disbelief.
'Thank you for telling me. That took courage.' Say it: it believes and validates.
'Don't worry, I won't tell anyone at all.' Avoid it: it promises secrecy you cannot keep.
Replace it with: 'I can't keep this fully secret, but I'll only tell those who need to know to help you.'
'You must report this to the police today.' Avoid it: the survivor decides what happens next, and you explain the options.
worked_example.answer: Swap disbelief, blanket secrecy and pressure for thanks, honest limits and options.

mistakes: Investigating, questioning the alleged perpetrator or gathering evidence.
Reacting with visible shock or disgust, which can silence the survivor.
Asking why they did not leave, or what they wore.
Sharing the story with colleagues or in chat groups.

recall.q: Name the four survivor-centred principles.
recall.a: Safety, confidentiality, respect and non-discrimination.

recall.q: Why explain your reporting duty early?
recall.a: So the survivor can decide how much to share, and because you cannot promise secrecy you cannot keep.

recall.q: What comes first in the hours after a disclosure?
recall.a: Immediate safety, then medical care, referral with consent, and the report.

recall.q: How does a child's disclosure differ?
recall.a: Best interests and mandatory legal reporting shape the response, and you cannot keep it confidential as you could for an adult.

sections.title: Reporting
sections.big_idea: A report must be **safe, known and possible**. Report the concern, protect the person, and never leave the reporter to face retaliation.
in_plain_words: Offer several routes, communicated in local languages, reachable by the least powerful and including an option that bypasses the person a complaint might name. Confidentiality means need-to-know only, secure storage and consent to share, with data protection law applying. Referral pathways cover medical, psychosocial, legal and safety help, and should be mapped before you need them.

Report any concern, suspicion or incident to your focal point, with facts and no conclusions, and promptly. If the concern involves the focal point, use the alternative or whistleblowing route. Good-faith reporters must never be penalised, and retaliation is itself a serious violation. The hardest page is the clash between mandatory reporting and an adult survivor's wishes: be honest up front, separate reporting from services and **report the concern while protecting the person**.

key_terms.meaning: Reporting wrongdoing, including cover-ups, in the public interest.
Any punishment of someone who reported in good faith.
Sharing information only with those who need it, for a stated reason.
Accompanying or actively connecting a survivor to a service.
The mapped route to medical, psychosocial, legal and safety services.

worked_example.title: Choose the route
worked_example.setup: Invented: you suspect your district manager, who is also the safeguarding focal point, of trading rations for sex.
steps: What to report: any concern, suspicion or incident. You do not judge whether it is serious enough.
To whom: normally the focal point, but the concern involves that person, so use the alternative or whistleblowing route.
Standard: a reasonable concern in good faith. You need no proof.
Content: report facts, meaning what you saw or were told, with no theory of guilt.
Confidentiality: share only with those in the chain who need to know.
Protection: retaliation against you would be a serious safeguarding violation.
worked_example.answer: Use the whistleblowing route, report the facts promptly in good faith, and rely on the protection from retaliation.

mistakes: Running a hotline in one language, in office hours, answered by the manager it might concern.
Promising an adult total secrecy, or overriding their wishes without explaining why.
Handing over a phone number and hoping. Use a warm handover where possible.
Forgetting to monitor the reporter after a report.

recall.q: Name the four referral pathways.
recall.a: Medical or health, psychosocial, legal or justice, and safety or security.

recall.q: What standard applies to a whistleblower's concern?
recall.a: Good faith and a reasonable concern, with no need for proof.

recall.q: When does a request for secrecy not hold?
recall.a: For children, where best interests and legal duties override it.

recall.q: What is the first question on the reporting checklist?
recall.a: Is the survivor safe right now?

sections.title: Investigation and accountability
sections.big_idea: Investigation is a **specialist task**. Your role ends at reporting and supporting, fairness covers both parties, and the survivor stays informed.
in_plain_words: Trained, independent investigators establish the facts through a fair, confidential, documented process, on the balance of probabilities. It is separate from criminal justice, where a crime may have occurred and the survivor's choice and legal duties govern police referral. Amateur investigation destroys evidence, endangers the survivor and can void a fair process. Over-sharing during a case re-harms survivors.

Fairness runs both ways. The survivor gets safety, confidentiality and updates, and the subject of concern is treated as innocent until a finding, can respond, and faces interim measures that are not punishment. Substantiated SEAH brings proportionate and consistent consequences, from dismissal to criminal referral and disclosure through the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme, which stops 'pass the trash' hiring. **Learn from every case** with a root-cause review.

children.label: Criminal referral
items: Where the conduct is a crime

diagram.caption: consequences must be consistent at every rank

key_terms.meaning: The person against whom an allegation is made.
Steps such as suspension that protect people and process without pre-judging guilt.
The standard for deciding whether misconduct occurred.
The form a recruiter requests from a candidate's former employers.
Asking which gap in supervision, access, culture or recruitment allowed the harm.

worked_example.title: Handle a canteen question
worked_example.setup: Invented: an investigation is under way, and a colleague asks why the driver has been suspended.
steps: Interim measures protect the survivor and the process. A suspension does not pre-judge guilt.
Slide 81: resist the instinct to explain or reassure. Do not name anyone.
Say only that a matter is being handled through the proper process.
Do not discuss theories of guilt or 'what really happened' with anyone.
Keep any records you hold access-controlled and out of chat groups.
worked_example.answer: Give the single line that a matter is being handled through the proper process, and nothing more.

mistakes: Starting your own enquiry after receiving a disclosure.
Moving a powerful offender on without disclosure while dismissing a junior one.
Forgetting the survivor, who hears nothing and gets no support.
Treating the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme as a central list of offenders. It runs on requests for Statements of Conduct.

recall.q: Who should investigate, and to what standard?
recall.a: Trained, independent investigators, on the balance of probabilities.

recall.q: How far back does the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme cover?
recall.a: At least five years of employment history for relevant roles.

recall.q: Is a survivor's support conditional on cooperating?
recall.a: No. Support and continued assistance are never conditional.

recall.q: Name three common pitfalls.
recall.a: Amateur investigation, protecting the senior, over-sharing, ignoring retaliation, forgetting the survivor, or cover-up under 'reputation'.

sections.title: Prevention and culture
sections.big_idea: Prevention is **layered**: assess risk, hire safely, train everyone, appoint focal points, build complaints with communities, oversee partners and lead by example.
in_plain_words: Do a safeguarding risk assessment at design stage and revisit it as context changes: who is at risk, where power sits, risk points such as distributions and cash transfers, and the controls for each. Safe recruitment layers value-based screening, reference checks, Misconduct Disclosure Scheme checks and self-declaration, because no single check is enough and charisma is no substitute for vetting.

Train every person at induction and in refreshers, in local languages and through scenarios. Focal points must be trained, authorised, diverse and more than one. Build complaint mechanisms with communities and repeat a simple message that aid is always free. Responsibility flows down to partners and sub-grantees. Culture is the deepest layer: psychological safety, consistent enforcement and **no exceptions for stars**.

diagram.caption: six layers, strongest when all are present

key_terms.meaning: A systematic look at where and how harm could occur, with controls.
Vetting built into every step of hiring.
A signed statement of any prior findings, plus agreement to the code.
A trained, authorised person who makes reporting real.
Contract terms passing safeguarding standards through the delivery chain.
Staff can raise concerns without fear of blame or reprisal.

worked_example.title: Map risk and controls
worked_example.setup: Invented: a cash distribution in a remote camp, with one volunteer managing the beneficiary list.
steps: Who is at risk: women, children, people with disabilities and the displaced.
Where power sits: the volunteer controls the list, and so access to cash.
Risk points: registration and distribution, at a remote site with little oversight.
Controls from slide 87: segregated queues, female staff, complaint boxes, dual oversight.
If the volunteer works for a sub-grantee, add flow-down clauses and monitoring.
Revisit the assessment when the context, partners or programme change.
worked_example.answer: Dual control of the list, female staff, a complaint route and partner oversight, each placed on a named risk point.

mistakes: Hiring on charisma or gut feeling without references and misconduct checks.
Naming a focal point without training, time or authority.
Assuming a clean record means a safe hire where records are unreliable.
Treating a partner's staff as someone else's problem.

recall.q: What does the deck call the single most effective prevention measure?
recall.a: Not hiring people who pose a risk, through safe recruitment.

recall.q: Why layer several vetting measures?
recall.a: No single check is sufficient, and perpetrators can interview well.

recall.q: Why have more than one focal point?
recall.a: So a complaint about one of them is not stuck.

recall.q: What is the clearest sign of a healthy safeguarding culture?
recall.a: Reports flowing through safe channels and being handled well.

sections.title: In practice
sections.big_idea: Every scenario resolves with the same three moves: **protect safety, share only what is needed, ask your focal point**.
in_plain_words: Three scenarios test the rules. A woman hints that a volunteer asked for a favour to keep her on a list: listen, reassure, explain your duty, refer with consent and report without confronting anyone. A colleague's romance with a community member: apply the power-imbalance test and declare. An anonymous note about a driver: take it seriously and pass it on.

Risk concentrates wherever a staff member controls something people need and oversight is thin, from cash lists to water points, clinics, classrooms and job selection. Each has a control. The common mistakes come from good intentions without training, and each myth is a door that lets harm continue. **Keep the checklist within reach**, and when in doubt make the three moves.

nodes.label: Reassure
nodes.sub: not her fault; aid is her right

nodes.label: Explain your duty
nodes.sub: report, share only what is needed

key_terms.meaning: Aid, or the promise of it, traded for sex.
Ask whether one party controls the other's access to what they need.
A step that cuts risk while a concern is assessed, without presuming guilt.
A report with no name that deserves the same seriousness as a named one.
A place where a staff member controls access to something people need.

worked_example.title: Work scenario 2
worked_example.setup: Slide 98: a colleague says he is in a real relationship with an adult woman from the community his team serves.
steps: Apply the power-imbalance test: his organisation provides assistance she depends on.
Check the rule: ST/SGB/2003/13 says such relationships are strongly discouraged, and many codes prohibit them outright.
Advise him to declare it to management now, so the conflict of interest can be managed, for example by reassignment.
Explain that declaring protects both of them and the organisation.
If he refuses, you have a duty to raise the concern yourself.
worked_example.answer: Declaration and reassignment. 'We're in love' does not remove the power gap.

mistakes: Confronting the volunteer in scenario 1, or removing the woman from the list.
Dismissing the anonymous note because it has no name, date or clear handwriting.
Applying 'we're consenting adults' to a relationship with a beneficiary.
Letting an organisation's reputation or a valuable colleague outweigh a report.

recall.q: In scenario 1, why must you not cut her aid?
recall.a: That would be retaliation.

recall.q: How are grey areas resolved?
recall.a: By the power-imbalance test and by declaration.

recall.q: What pattern shows where risk concentrates?
recall.a: Wherever a staff member controls access to something people need and oversight is thin.

recall.q: What three moves rarely go wrong when in doubt?
recall.a: Protect the survivor's safety, share only what is needed, and ask your focal point.

notes.2: Read the five promises on this slide as your learning checklist: speak the language, know the red lines, receive a disclosure, report safely, build prevention in. The idea underneath all five is that people who use aid to exploit **rely on silence**, so safeguarding replaces silence with standards and safe reporting.
notes.3: The course is for everyone connected to the organisation, drivers and board members included, because duties do not stop at the payroll edge. It complements your own policy and focal point and does not replace them. The slide also gives permission: **pause if any part is distressing**.
notes.5: Failures rarely come from a missing policy. They come from ordinary staff who missed a warning sign, did not know how to receive a disclosure or did not report. You are the frontline, you hold power, and you may be the only witness, so **safeguarding is the job**.
notes.6: Remember the umbrella: child protection, protection of at-risk adults and protection from SEAH sit under safeguarding, all flowing from do no harm. It overlaps with child protection, GBV response, HR conduct and duty of care but is bigger than any one of them. Read it as **about the people we serve**.
notes.7: Use the table as a map of the course. Parts 1 and 2 give language, Part 3 the reasons, Part 4 the standards, Part 5 the red lines, then receiving, reporting, investigating, preventing and practising. Your own policy and code sit on top of these global standards.
notes.8: Treat this glossary as a map and read the later parts for the detail. Hold on to two points: PSEA covers harm to the people served while SEAH is the umbrella for all of it, and 'survivor' replaces 'victim' to stress agency and recovery. A focal point is a person and a referral pathway is a route.
notes.9: Safeguarding protects two overlapping groups: the people we serve and the people we work with. The first is PSEA, harm by staff to affected populations. The second is sexual harassment between colleagues. The distinction decides **which policy, channel and response applies**, so learn it now.
notes.10: The reframe is the heart of the course: ask 'was there a power imbalance?' as your first question. When one person controls food, shelter, a job or a grade, apparent consent cannot be freely given. **Every red line closes off a way power becomes sexual gain.**
notes.11: Four word choices to adopt: survivor, alleged until proven, believe without judging, and no blaming language. Receiving a disclosure is not investigating it. Words are part of safety, since **careless words close mouths that a careful word would open**.
notes.12: Memorise these five ground rules and the rest of the course follows from them. The first, **it can happen here**, matters most, because 'not in our organisation' lets harm continue. Notice the fourth: silence that shields an abuser is complicity, while discretion about a survivor is sacred.
notes.14: Safeguarding has three actions: prevent, report and respond, learn. Use that as a frame for the rest of the course. It covers all forms of harm, but this course concentrates on the sexual harms grouped as SEAH, **where the sector's failures have been gravest**.
notes.15: Note the direction of PSEA: an aid provider harming the people the aid is meant to help. That is the particular betrayal it names. The UN formalised the term in 2003 after abuses in West Africa. Use PSEA when the person harmed is an **affected person**.
notes.16: The definition turns on abuse of a power gap, with or without force. Use the three examples: demanding sex for a place on a list, transactional sex with an affected person, and trafficking or enabling. **Money changing hands does not make it acceptable**; the exchange is what is prohibited.
notes.17: Keep exploitation and abuse apart. Exploitation abuses a position of power or trust for sexual purposes. Abuse is the physical intrusion itself, including coerced acts where consent is extracted by threat, deception or unequal conditions. They often occur together, and both are **serious misconduct and usually crimes**.
notes.18: Sexual harassment usually runs between colleagues. Learn the four forms: verbal, non-verbal, physical and quid pro quo. In India the PoSH Act 2013 governs it and requires an Internal Committee in every eligible workplace. Sort any case by **who is harmed**, and that tells you the route.
notes.19: Name the imbalance and the rules make sense. The three kinds of power are positional, relational and situational, and one person often holds more than one. Because agreement can be coerced without a single threat, the rules **prohibit the conduct outright** and skip the question of whether she agreed.
notes.20: This is the key table of Part 2. Compare who is harmed, who causes it, the power gap, the policy and the standard. **Misfiling a beneficiary's complaint into HR**, or the reverse, can leave a survivor unprotected, so route by the question: who is harmed, and by whom?
notes.21: Read the umbrella as an equation: exploitation plus abuse plus harassment equals SEAH. SEA targets affected people and falls under PSEA. SH targets colleagues and falls under workplace policy. Donor contracts use SEAH to cover all three, so ask **who is being harmed, and by whom**.
notes.22: A child is anyone under 18, whatever the local age of majority or consent. No consent is possible, and mistaken age is no defence. POCSO 2012 adds mandatory reporting, a legal layer on top of every policy. Child safeguarding is **its own discipline** across all programme contact.
notes.23: Protection extends to adults at heightened risk: people in crisis, people with disabilities, women and girls, and marginalised groups who may distrust formal systems. The last line is the lesson: **vulnerability is created by situations**, and your programme can reduce it or deepen it.
notes.25: Study the timeline: misconduct in 2010–11, an internal inquiry that was not made public, The Times in February 2018, and the Charity Commission report in June 2019. The lesson is in the handling. A flawed investigation and **cover-up compounded harm**, as much as the abuse itself.
notes.26: 2018 turned a scandal into a sector-wide reckoning: a parliamentary inquiry, the London Safeguarding Summit, the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme and donor conditions. Safeguarding capacity became a condition of funding. Remember the motto: **no charity is more important than the people it serves** or the mission it pursues.
notes.27: Do no harm is the foundation stone. Aid arrives in moments of acute need and dependence, which is what makes it a vector for exploitation if unsafeguarded. Use the slide's closing question as your test: **how do we make sure the people we came to help are never harmed by us?**
notes.28: Power concentrates in providers: a single ration card or cash transfer can decide a family's survival. Compare the two lists, what the provider holds and what the recipient faces. Because the gap is so wide, prohibiting the conduct is **the only reliable protection**.
notes.29: Six reasons keep survivors silent: fear of losing aid, retaliation, stigma, no safe channel, disbelief and normalisation. Read the last line as a rule: few reports are no evidence of low prevalence. **Silence is the perpetrator's greatest ally**, so fix channels before you celebrate low numbers.
notes.30: Donors now screen for safeguarding. List what they expect: a written policy and code, named responsibility, safe recruitment, flow-down clauses and incident reporting within timelines. For a South Asian NGO this is an ethical duty and a **practical condition of funding**, including increasingly domestic and CSR money.
notes.31: Count the cost in order: human cost first, organisational cost second. Oxfam's response shows prevention is cheaper than the aftermath. The slide's last warning is the one to keep: **never protect reputation at a survivor's expense**, because the damage from a cover-up is always worse.
notes.32: Five features of South Asian contexts concentrate the risk: deep inequality, recurrent crises, a large informal workforce, strong stigma and distrust of formal systems. They make **locally designed, community-based and confidential** complaint mechanisms essential. Use the list to audit your own programme setting.
notes.33: Follow the four stages from denial to a culture where it is safe to speak. Zero tolerance means zero tolerance of inaction and promises no absence of incidents. A **rising number of reports** through safe channels is often a sign the system is working.
notes.35: Use this table as the index to Part 4. Five instruments, each with a job: IASC principles for conduct, the Bulletin for definitions, the CHS for accountability, the Disclosure Scheme for recruitment, national law as the binding floor. Your own code sits on top.
notes.36: Learn principles 1 to 3: gross misconduct, no sex with children, no exchange for sex. Notice the details that close loopholes: age rules apply regardless of the local age of consent, mistaken belief is no defence, and the exchange ban includes **assistance that is due** to beneficiaries.
notes.37: Principles 4 to 6: no relationships that abuse power, a duty to report, and a duty to sustain the environment. The closing line is the lesson: **refraining from harm yourself falls short**. You must report others' harm and help build a culture that prevents it.
notes.38: The Bulletin is the common ancestor of the IASC principles and most codes of conduct. Remember its sections: 1 defines, 3 prohibits, 6 extends the standards to partners and contractors. When a policy cites 'the SG Bulletin', **this is the document it means**.
notes.39: The CHS has nine commitments on quality and accountability to affected people. Two matter most here: the commitment that support does no harm, and the one on safely reporting complaints. The six lines on the slide group the nine, with the last covering several, so **read them as a set**.
notes.40: Test any complaint mechanism against four words: known, accessible, safe and confidential, responsive. The last paragraph is the warning: a mechanism that does not **explicitly welcome and safely route SEAH complaints** will miss them, because those are the complaints people fear most.
notes.41: Reporting is mandatory, applies across agencies and covers suspicion. You are the reporter and the investigator's job is separate, so you need no certainty. Silence is not neutral and can be a disciplinary matter. Hold the tension with confidentiality by **reporting the concern while protecting the survivor's safety and choices**.
notes.42: Duty of care runs in both directions: to the people served and to staff and volunteers. The three bullets turn it into accountability: boards and senior managers own safeguarding, budgets and expertise must be real, and the duty is continuous. **Good intentions become enforceable responsibility.**
notes.43: Memorise the nesting order: Bulletin for definitions, IASC for conduct rules, CHS for accountability to communities, your policy for local rules. The instruments fit together and none competes with another. Day to day, **your own code and national law bind you**, drawing authority from the global standards.
notes.45: Learn the five red lines: under 18, exchange for sex, relationships with beneficiaries, harassment, and the duty to report. They are absolute and crossing them is serious misconduct whatever the context, consent claims or seniority. Staff must **understand where the lines are**, or a policy sits in a drawer.
notes.46: Three details make this red line absolute: local age of consent does not matter, a mistaken belief about age does not matter, and programme contact counts. In India POCSO makes reporting a legal duty. If you are unsure whether someone is over 18, **treat them as a child**.
notes.47: Exchange covers money, jobs, food, transport, favours and assistance already owed. 'Paid' does not make it acceptable, because the power gap makes it exploitation. Withholding entitlements as pressure and turning a blind eye also breach the code. This is **the conduct the whole PSEA framework was built to stop**.
notes.48: The Bulletin says such relationships are 'strongly discouraged', and many organisations go further and prohibit them or require declaration and reassignment. The key point is that consent cannot be verified where one party holds power over aid. If a relationship arises, **declare it** and let the organisation manage the conflict.
notes.49: A conflict of interest is where exploitation hides. The four examples are beneficiary selection, local hiring, procurement and cash, and dual relationships. The rule is three words: **declare, don't decide**. Tell your manager and step back from the decision. Declaring protects you as much as the community.
notes.50: Gifts create obligation, blur boundaries and can groom or buy silence, in whichever direction they travel. Accepting from people who depend on you signals that access can be bought, and giving to chosen individuals is a classic grooming pattern. Aid is **delivered fairly and never granted as a favour**.
notes.51: The same red lines apply online. Four rules: no sexual or exploitative content, no private unsupervised messaging with beneficiaries, recognise online grooming, and never store survivor data on personal devices or informal chat groups. **A message can exploit as surely as a meeting.**
notes.52: Photos need informed consent in a language the person understands, and they can decline without losing assistance. For children, obtain consent from the child and a guardian. Show people with dignity as agents. **Consent for a photo does not last for ever**, so honour removal requests.
notes.53: The code gathers the red lines into one signed document. Four features: signed on joining and reaffirmed, applied everywhere including online and off duty, binding partners too, and carrying consequences up to dismissal and criminal referral. **Read your own code** and ask your focal point before you are in the field.
notes.54: Most safeguarding is ordinary boundary-keeping. Meet in open places, keep contact professional, treat everyone equally, and model it for juniors. Use the test at the bottom: **would you be comfortable if your manager, the community and the survivor's family saw exactly what you are doing?** If not, do not do it.
notes.56: Signs come as patterns, in a power holder and in an affected person. Read both lists, then the caution: signs prove nothing alone. They are **prompts to pay attention** and, where a concern forms, to report and to hold back from accusing. Trust your unease enough to raise it through the proper channel.
notes.57: Learn the four shapes of disclosure: direct, hinted, third-party and behavioural. A person may test you with a small disclosure first, so **your reaction to the first hint** decides whether the full story is told. Treat every hint as important and respond calmly.
notes.58: Memorise the four principles: safety, confidentiality, respect, non-discrimination. They are the standard across GBV and PSEA response and resolve most dilemmas. When unsure what to do after a disclosure, ask which action best serves each of the four, and begin with **the survivor's safety**.
notes.59: Five practices put the principles to work: believe and validate, restore control, offer informed choice, do no further harm, and safety over process. Abuse takes control away, so your response must give it back. In the hard case, be honest and **never promise absolute secrecy you cannot keep**.
notes.60: Use this list as a sequence: private space, patient listening, belief, honesty about confidentiality, safety question, honest options, referral, minimal record. You do not need to be an expert. Your job is to **receive with care and connect the survivor** to those who are.
notes.61: The most common harm after a disclosure comes from well-meaning responders who investigate, gossip or over-promise. Go through the seven refusals: no secrecy promises, no investigation, no blame, no visible shock, no forced decisions, no sharing, no photos. **Restraint is part of care.**
notes.62: Rehearse the left column aloud until it feels natural. Each right-hand phrase shows a failure: disbelief, delay-blame, victim-blame, pressure, a false promise, an interrogation. You do not need perfect words. **Warmth, calm and honesty** matter more, and a survivor remembers how safe you made them feel.
notes.63: With a child the survivor-centred principles still apply, but best interests and mandatory reporting under POCSO shape the response. Do not promise secrecy, do not interview, and involve guardians carefully unless one may be the source of harm. **Know your procedure and legal duty beforehand.**
notes.64: Receiving disclosures is heavy, and a depleted responder cannot help survivors. Debrief with your focal point or supervisor without gossip, know your limits as a first responder and a bridge to services, access support and watch for the signs. **Self-care is part of the safeguarding system**.
notes.65: Follow the four steps in order: safety, medical care, referral with consent, then the report. Time matters for some post-assault care, so offer referral urgently without forcing it. **Move with urgency on safety and health, and with patience on the rest**, because the survivor sets the pace.
notes.67: Design channels for the people least able to use them. Offer several routes, make them known in local languages, make them accessible to the least powerful, keep them confidential and include one that bypasses the person a complaint might be about. A hotline answered by the district manager **will never surface a complaint** against that manager.
notes.68: Confidentiality means need-to-know, with the fewest people and a reason for each. No identifying details in email, chat or shared drives, secure storage, and consent before sharing. Data protection law applies, so treat survivor information as the most sensitive data you hold. **One careless breach can destroy trust in the whole system.**
notes.69: Four kinds of help: medical, psychosocial, legal and safety. Medical care is often time-critical. A pathway helps only if it exists before you need it, so **map the nearest services in advance**, keep the list current, and know the clinic, One Stop Centre, counsellor, legal aid and helpline.
notes.70: A referral is survivor-centred when the survivor consents, information is minimal, and the service treats them with the same care you did. Prefer a warm handover and follow up on safety. Helplines such as 181 and 1098 are common, so **verify local availability and reliability** before relying on any one.
notes.71: Whistleblowing differs from a survivor's disclosure: it is reporting wrongdoing, including cover-ups or abuse by senior staff, in the public interest. You need a reasonable concern in good faith, and no proof. It gives staff a safe route **when the people above them are the problem**.
notes.72: Retaliation is itself a serious safeguarding violation, whether against a beneficiary (cutting off aid) or staff (dismissal, demotion, threats). Monitor actively after a report. A single unaddressed act can undo years of trust, because **protecting reporters is what makes reporting possible at all**.
notes.73: Report any concern, suspicion, allegation or witnessed incident, and do not judge whether it is serious enough. Go to your focal point or the channel in your policy, or the alternative route if the concern involves them. Report facts promptly and share only what is needed. **When unsure, report.**
notes.74: This is the hardest page. Both the duty and the survivor's autonomy are real, so manage the tension openly: be honest up front, separate reporting from services, report the concern and protect the person, and seek guidance. Children differ because their **best interests and legal duties** override secrecy.
notes.75: Use the ten questions as a pocket card for the moments after a disclosure: safety, medical care, channel, honesty, minimum information, accurate record, no investigation, referral, protection of the reporter, and child duties. **Structure prevents the mistakes** that good intentions alone do not.
notes.77: Investigation is a specialist task. Trained, independent investigators run a fair, confidential, documented fact-finding, separate from the criminal process. Your role ends at reporting and supporting. **Amateur investigation destroys evidence, endangers survivors and can void a fair process**, however well-meaning it is.
notes.78: Fairness runs both ways. The survivor needs safety, confidentiality, support and updates. The subject of concern needs to be treated as innocent until a finding, to know the allegation and to respond. **Interim measures are not punishment**: they protect the survivor and the process without pre-judging guilt.
notes.79: Consequences must be proportionate and consistent, so seniority never buys immunity: discipline up to dismissal, criminal referral where the conduct is a crime, a record for future references, systemic fixes and donor notification. The test of consistency is whether **a senior offender faces the same disclosure** as a junior one.
notes.80: Closing the loop is part of the duty of care. Keep the survivor informed as far as confidentiality and fairness allow, continue support after the investigation ends, and never make assistance depend on cooperating. A survivor who hears nothing feels abandoned, and the community learns that reporting is **pointless**.
notes.81: Investigations run on information discipline. Five rules: need-to-know, no naming, no speculation, secure records and a consistent line. If asked, say only that a matter is being handled through the proper process. **Over-sharing is one of the commonest ways survivors are re-harmed.**
notes.82: The Scheme stops 'pass the trash' hiring. It sets a minimum standard for sharing substantiated SEAH findings in recruitment, uses a Statement of Conduct requested from former employers, covers at least five years and gives a legally sound template. It is a request process and holds **no central list of offenders**.
notes.83: Much SEAH is also a crime, and an internal investigation does not replace the criminal justice system. Child sexual abuse must be reported under POCSO, and failure to report is itself an offence. For adults, the survivor's informed choice guides referral. **When in doubt on a criminal matter, seek legal advice immediately.**
notes.84: Accountability covers the organisation as well as the individual. Run a root-cause review, update controls, share anonymised lessons, track trends and report transparently to boards and donors. Organisations that treat each case as a threat to bury **repeat their failures** and betray the people they serve.
notes.85: Six pitfalls: amateur investigation, protecting the senior, over-sharing, ignoring retaliation, forgetting the survivor and cover-up under 'reputation'. Notice how many are cultural, and few are technical. A fair, survivor-centred, transparent culture prevents most of them, which is **the subject of Part 9**.
notes.87: A safeguarding risk assessment is as basic as a security or financial one. Walk through the questions: who is at risk, where power sits, risk points, contextual risk and controls. Do it at design stage and revisit it, because **risk is dynamic**. Examples of controls include segregated queues and dual oversight.
notes.88: The single most effective prevention measure is not hiring people who pose a risk. Use five layers: value-based screening, references on conduct, Misconduct Disclosure Scheme checks, identity and gap checks, and depth in proportion to the role. **A charismatic candidate is not a vetted candidate**.
notes.89: No single check is enough, so layer references, a misconduct check, a signed declaration and a probing interview. Background checks vary widely across South Asia and must never be relied on alone. Where records are poor, **make references and the Scheme non-negotiable** and document what you did.
notes.90: A policy no one has read prevents nothing. Train at induction before field contact, refresh at least annually, go deeper for focal points and managers, use local languages and formats, and teach through scenarios. Reaching everyone matters, and **headquarters is no exception**, as Oxfam's mandatory training shows.
notes.91: A focal point is the human infrastructure of reporting. Check five things: known and reachable, trained, authorised with time and backing, diverse and more than one, and connected to referral and investigators. A focal point in name only is **worse than none**, since it looks like a system.
notes.92: Build complaint mechanisms with communities as co-designers. Raise awareness that aid is free, offer multiple routes, close the feedback loop and coordinate across agencies. Repeat a simple message everywhere: **aid is always free** and no one may ask for anything in exchange, least of all sex.
notes.93: Responsibility flows down the whole delivery chain. Assess partners before funding, use flow-down clauses, build capacity, offer joint reporting routes and monitor. Support smaller local partners to develop safeguarding as well as setting conditions. **'It was the partner's staff' is no defence**; donors and communities hold the whole chain accountable.
notes.94: Culture is the deepest layer of prevention and the hardest to fake. Look for five signs: psychological safety, consistent enforcement, openness about incidents, everyday challenge of inappropriate jokes and questioning of power. **Reports flowing through safe channels** and handled well are the clearest sign of health. Silence is the danger sign.
notes.95: Leadership sets the tone. Board accountability, real resources, modelled behaviour and no exceptions for stars are the four marks. The most damaging signal is protecting a valuable but abusive colleague. Every serious failure the sector examined traces partly to **leaders who put reputation or a star performer first**.
notes.97: Work the scenario before reading the resolution. The right response is private space, calm listening, reassurance, an honest statement of your duty, safety questions, referral with consent and a report to the focal point. Then check what you must avoid: confronting the volunteer, promising secrecy, gossip, **or cutting her aid**.
notes.98: Grey areas resolve with the power-imbalance test and declaration. The colleague's 'we're both consenting adults' ignores that the woman depends on his organisation's assistance. Advise declaration and reassignment, and raise it yourself if he refuses. **'We're in love' does not remove the power gap.**
notes.99: An anonymous, vague note is still serious. Anonymity reflects how unsafe reporting feels. Pass it to the focal point, do not question anyone yourself, consider interim safety steps without pre-judging guilt, and strengthen safe reporting so more can come forward. Treat it with **the same seriousness as a named report**.
notes.100: Find the control point in each sector: lists and payments in cash and food, isolated facilities in WASH, private contact in health, trusted access to children in education, selection in livelihoods. The pattern repeats wherever **staff control access and oversight is thin**. Map those points in your programme and put a control on each.
notes.101: Read this as reflexes to practise: be honest about reporting duties, leave investigation to trained staff, assume under-reporting, keep strict need-to-know, enforce consistently, support the survivor and own the whole chain. Almost every mistake comes from good intentions without training, so **learn the right reflex in advance**.
notes.102: Test your own thinking against each myth. 'It couldn't happen here', 'she was paid' and 'they consented' are the most dangerous, because each excuses a power gap. Low reporting usually means unsafe channels. Closing each myth in your own mind is **the first act of prevention**.
notes.103: Use the FAQ as a quick decision guide. If unsure, report. If the concern is your manager, use the alternative route. If a survivor asks for secrecy, be honest and share the minimum. Suspicion is enough. The closing three moves: **protect safety, share only what is needed, ask your focal point**.
notes.104: Turn this into a personal audit: do you know the red lines, your code, your focal point and the alternative, the referral pathway, how to receive and report well, how to protect reporters, and how to build prevention and model culture? Safeguarding is a set of **everyday habits**.
notes.105: Pair each source with its job: the Bulletin for definitions, the IASC principles for the baseline, the CHS for safe complaints, the Hub for practical tools, the Disclosure Scheme for recruitment, the Charity Commission report for the case, and national law. Above all, **read your own policy and code**.
notes.106: Eight takeaways, one theme: power. Start with the first and the last: safeguarding is everyone's job, and when in doubt you protect safety, share only what is needed and report to your focal point. Use the middle six as a revision list for the red lines, response, reporting and prevention.
